img_c39e3df610ea24d9.description: A crosshatched artist's sketch of the bearded frontiersman in his wide-brimmed hat — not a photograph, and not a portrait from life. No verified photograph or documented life portrait of Weaver exists, so this is an imagined commemorative likeness, most plausibly drawn in the 1920s. Powell 'Pauline' Weaver, Tennessee-born trapper, scout and prospector of part-Cherokee descent, petitioned Mexican authorities in 1845 (with partner Isaac Williams) for possession of the abandoned Rancho San Gorgonio, lived in an adobe near the future Beaumont running cattle in the pass, and conveyed the ranch to Dr. Isaac W. Smith before leaving in 1857; he later sparked the 1862 La Paz gold rush, camped at the future site of Prescott, and died at Camp Verde, Arizona Territory, on June 21, 1867. He is buried on the Sharlot Hall Museum grounds in Prescott.
corrections: The old caption 'c. 1850s-1860s' implied a photograph from life — no verified photograph of Weaver is known to exist; the defensible claim is 'posthumous likeness', likely 1920s.
